I am 60 years old, and I have been farming these fields in Quzhou for over forty years. My family has 6 mu of flat, irrigable land. I finished middle school, so I can read the seed bags and follow the county extension leaflets, but at the end of the day I trust what I have seen with my own eyes. This autumn I will sow winter wheat on the full 6 mu, because wheat has a guaranteed market and the county grain station buys it every June without haggling. I will use Luyuan 502, an improved variety that my neighbours have had good luck with for the last several seasons. Before sowing I will have the plot rotary-tilled. For fertilizer I will spread 100 kg of compound fertilizer per mu as a basal dose, and topdress with another 50 kg of urea in the spring—altogether that works out to about 22 kg of nitrogen, 10 kg of phosphorus and 5 kg of potassium per mu. I will irrigate four times: the winter-irrigation after sowing, the green-up water in March, the jointing water and the grain-filling water. I will spray pesticide three times, mainly for aphids and fusarium head blight. I expect about 1,050 kg per mu if the spring frost stays away. Immediately after harvesting the wheat in early June, I will no-till plant summer maize on the same 6 mu. I will sow Denghai 605, a hybrid seed that I buy from the cooperative every year. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat; I will put down 80 kg of compound fertilizer per mu at planting, which gives roughly 18 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus and 4 kg potassium per mu. I will irrigate twice, at the jointing stage and the filling stage, and spray pesticide three times for corn borer and weeds. I expect about 1,100 kg per mu. I am not planting cotton this year. At my age my back aches after long hours of pruning and picking, and the wheat-maize rotation can be managed almost entirely with hired machinery, which my son arranges for me.
